Your teacher covers the three kinds of plate boundary and the evidence for plate tectonics in class. These questions check the basics.

## Moving apart

```step
stage: investigate
insight: "Node 3: divergent boundaries, mid-ocean ridges and seafloor spreading, crust youngest at the ridge."
tasks:
  - check: {"type":"question","q":"Two oceanic plates move apart. What forms at the gap?","options":["A mid-ocean ridge, as magma rises and cools into new crust","A deep trench","A fold mountain range","An earthquake zone only, with no new rock"],"answer":0,"feedback":[null,"Trenches form where plates collide and one sinks.","Fold mountains form where continents collide.","New crust forms too, which is why the seafloor spreads."],"explain":"Tension lets magma rise into the gap, where it cools into new oceanic crust. Over time this builds a ridge and spreads the seafloor."}
  - check: {"type":"question","q":"You collect rock from the seafloor at the ridge and from far away on either side. Where is the rock youngest?","options":["At the ridge, getting older with distance","Far from the ridge, getting younger towards the ridge","The same age everywhere","Youngest on one side only"],"answer":0,"feedback":[null,"That would mean the crust is being made far away.","The ages are not all the same; they follow a pattern.","The pattern is the same on both sides of the ridge."],"explain":"New crust forms at the ridge and moves away, so the oldest crust is furthest from it."}
  - check: {"type":"reflect","text":"I can say what happens where plates move apart and where the youngest ocean crust is found."}
```

## Colliding

```step
stage: investigate
insight: "Node 4: subduction, trenches and volcanic arcs; continent collisions make mountains."
tasks:
  - check: {"type":"question","q":"An oceanic plate meets a continental plate. What happens?","options":["The denser oceanic plate sinks beneath the continent (subduction), forming a trench and a line of volcanoes","Both plates sink equally","The plates slide sideways past each other","Both plates stop moving"],"answer":0,"feedback":[null,"They are not equally dense, so one sinks.","Sliding past is a transform boundary.","Plates keep moving; the stress is released over time."],"explain":"Oceanic crust is denser, so it sinks. A deep trench forms at the bend, and melting above the sinking plate feeds a volcanic arc."}
  - check: {"type":"question","q":"Why does a collision between two continents make mountains rather than subduction?","options":["Both are light, buoyant crust, so neither sinks easily and the rock crumples upwards","Continental crust is denser than the mantle, so it sinks","One continent always slides under the other, as ocean crust does","The plates stop moving when they meet"],"answer":0,"feedback":[null,"If it were denser than the mantle it would sink, and it doesn't.","Continental crust is too buoyant to sink far, so it piles up instead.","They keep pushing, which is what folds the rock upwards."],"explain":"Continental crust is too light to sink far. The collision squeezes and folds the rock upwards, as in the Himalayas."}
  - check: {"type":"reflect","text":"I can describe subduction, the trench and volcanic arc it makes, and why continents colliding make mountains."}
```

## Sliding past

```step
stage: investigate
insight: "Node 5: transform boundaries, stress and earthquakes without volcanoes."
tasks:
  - check: {"type":"question","q":"Two plates slide past each other along a transform boundary. Why do earthquakes happen there?","options":["The plates stick, stress builds, and the rock suddenly slips and releases it","The plates melt","Magma pushes the plates apart","The plates stop moving"],"answer":0,"feedback":[null,"Plates slide past without melting.","Magma rising is a feature of divergent boundaries.","They keep moving; they just get stuck and then slip."],"explain":"Friction locks the plates for a while. When the stress becomes too great, the rock slips and the energy is released as an earthquake."}
  - check: {"type":"question","q":"Do transform boundaries have volcanoes?","options":["Usually not, because plates are neither pulling apart nor sinking, so magma does not form","Yes, many large ones","Yes, but only in the ocean","Yes, because of friction"],"answer":0,"feedback":[null,"Not usually; there is no process to make magma.","The ocean makes no difference.","Friction releases energy as earthquakes, not melts rock."],"explain":"Volcanoes need magma. Sliding past does not make a gap for magma to rise or push a plate down into the mantle to melt."}
  - check: {"type":"sort","q":"Which kind of boundary is it?","options":["Divergent","Convergent","Transform"],"items":[["Mid-ocean ridge","Divergent"],["Ocean trench","Convergent"],["San Andreas Fault in California","Transform","Plates slide sideways past each other."],["Himalayas","Convergent"],["East African Rift","Divergent"]]}
  - check: {"type":"reflect","text":"I can describe a transform boundary and explain why it has earthquakes but not volcanoes."}
```

## Evidence

```step
stage: investigate
insight: "Node 6: at least three independent lines of evidence and what each shows; seafloor age is the strongest."
tasks:
  - check: {"type":"sort","q":"Is it evidence that the plates have moved?","options":["Evidence","Not evidence"],"items":[["The coastlines of South America and Africa fit together","Evidence"],["The same fossils on continents now separated by ocean","Evidence","They were once joined, so the same plants and animals lived on both."],["The seafloor is youngest at the mid-ocean ridges","Evidence"],["Earthquakes and volcanoes line up along plate edges","Evidence"],["The Moon has craters","Not evidence","It tells us about impacts, not about plates moving."]]}
  - check: {"type":"question","q":"Which evidence most strongly shows the seafloor is spreading from ridges?","options":["The pattern of rock ages: young at the ridge, older with distance, the same on both sides","Coastlines that look alike","The size of the oceans","Earthquakes along the ridges"],"answer":0,"feedback":[null,"Coastlines suggest the continents fit, but not how the seafloor moves.","Size alone does not show movement.","Earthquakes show the ridge is active, but not that the floor moves outwards from it."],"explain":"The matching age pattern on both sides is what spreading predicts, and is hard to explain any other way."}
  - check: {"type":"match","q":"Match each piece of evidence to what it shows.","pairs":[["Coastlines of South America and Africa fit","The continents were once joined"],["The same fossils on continents now far apart","The same plants and animals once lived on connected land"],["Seafloor youngest at the ridges","New crust forms at the ridges and spreads outwards"],["Earthquakes and volcanoes in lines","Where plates meet and move against each other"]]}
  - check: {"type":"reflect","text":"I can give three lines of evidence for plate tectonics and say what each one shows."}
```

### I can

```teacher
summary: A self-test on divergent, convergent and transform boundaries and the
  evidence for plate tectonics (AC9S8U03, nodes 3 to 6, taught in class; node 6
  a hinge).
time: 18
timing: Nodes 3 to 5 4 min each · Evidence 6 min
goals:
  - I can say what forms at each kind of plate boundary.
  - I can explain why earthquakes happen at transform boundaries.
  - I can give three lines of evidence for plate tectonics.
before: >
  A Quick check: a few questions on what students should know for AC9S8U03 nodes
  3 to 6, which you teach in class. It has no board, no clip and no new
  teaching, and it is optional, so it never holds up course completion. Set the
  width with `?width=minimum`, `typical` (default) or `wider`.


  Use it as a self-test after your teaching, a starter, or revision. The Layers
  and What moves the plates lessons on screen come first (nodes 1 and 2); these
  are the boundaries and evidence you teach in class. Students can do one node
  at a time.
running:
  - 'Do each boundary as a pair: a question and the "I can" line.'
  - Finish with the Which boundary sort and the evidence sort, then ask for a
    third line of evidence out loud.
struggle: Keeping the three boundaries apart. When a student mixes them up, ask
  which way the plates are moving relative to each other.
stuck:
  - see: A student says earthquakes move the plates.
    ask: Which comes first, the plates moving or the earthquake?
    fix: The plates move and get stuck; the earthquake is the release of stress.
  - see: A student says trenches form where plates move apart.
    ask: Which way is the plate moving at a trench?
    fix: "Together, with one sinking: subduction."
stretch: Choose a place (Japan, Iceland, the Andes, the Himalayas). Name its
  boundary type and two features that show it.
support: Give a diagram of the three boundaries with arrows showing plate
  movement to label.
leads: >
  Back in class: model the boundaries with trays or modelling clay; plot recent
  earthquakes and volcanoes on a world map.
exit:
  q: Name the three kinds of plate boundary and one feature of each.
  a: "Divergent: mid-ocean ridge. Convergent: trench, volcanic arc or fold
    mountains. Transform: earthquakes along a fault."
explain: >
  Where plates **move apart** (divergent), magma rises and makes new crust, so
  the seafloor is youngest at the ridge. Where they **collide** (convergent),
  denser ocean crust sinks (subduction) to make trenches and volcanic arcs; two
  continents crumple into mountains. Where they **slide past** (transform),
  stress builds and is released as earthquakes.


  Evidence: fitting coastlines, matching fossils and rocks, the age pattern of
  the seafloor, and the lines of earthquakes and volcanoes.
```
